description: Prisma Client: which types are clients of the database, and what each client operation reads and writes.

rules.description: PrismaClient, as @prisma/client exports it, is a client of the database; so is a project class that extends it, as a NestJS PrismaService does.
rules.why: A call on a client's model delegate, prisma.user.findMany(...), is SQL the client sends to the table of that model.

examples.source:
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';
export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient {}

import { PrismaClient as Db } from '@prisma/client';
export class Store extends Db {}
examples.why: the import is matched by what the package exports, not by the local name

examples.source:
import { PrismaClient } from './my-own-client';
export class NotPrisma extends PrismaClient {}
examples.why: a class of that name from another module is not Prisma's

rules.description: PrismaService, as the nestjs-prisma package exports it, is a client of the database: the package declares it as a class extending PrismaClient.
rules.why: nestjs-prisma-starter injects nestjs-prisma's PrismaService; the source never shows that it is a PrismaClient, because it is in a package.

library.declares: export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient<Prisma.PrismaClientOptions, 'query' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'> implements OnModuleInit
library.source: nestjs-prisma, lib/prisma.service.ts, re-exported by lib/index.ts, read on main (github.com/notiz-dev/nestjs-prisma); nestjs-prisma-starter pins 0.22.0-dev.0

examples.source:
import { PrismaService } from 'nestjs-prisma';
export class Db extends PrismaService {}

rules.description: What each Prisma Client model operation is, and what part each argument plays: select returns the fields set to true (a value that is neither true nor false MAY be returned, read at run time), where and cursor filter by the fields they name (through the combinators AND, OR and NOT), orderBy, distinct, by and the aggregates read theirs, data, create and update write theirs, and include reaches relations. A key naming a compound unique or id (schema.prisma's @@unique/@@id) is read through the model's own compounds, never by splitting the key. A relation is followed into its model: in include or select as a find of its own (true is its whole row), in a filter through some, every, none, is and isNot (or a to-one filter written straight), _count as the related rows it counts, and in data as the nested writes it names, each with what it does to the related rows and to the link. A relation filtered on null (the relation written null, or is or isNot given null) only checks the link. A nested write handed a literal that makes it do nothing (create: [], connect: [], disconnect: false on a one-to-one, delete: false, deleteMany: [], ...) is not followed, and set replaces the link, so set: [] clears it. $extends on a client makes a client, and an extension with a query component, or one not read, may change what a call sends; an extension Prisma.defineExtension makes is read where the same method holds it; a field its result component computes reads the fields its needs names.
rules.why: Prisma Client's model API (prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-client-reference): a find without select returns every scalar field of the model, include returns every scalar field of the related model, and a nested write (create, connect, connectOrCreate, set, disconnect, update, updateMany, upsert, delete, deleteMany) acts on the related rows and on the link between the two. Client extensions (prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/client-extensions): $extends returns a new client, and its query component intercepts the operations it names; a result component's field is computed on the client from the fields its needs sets to true, which Prisma selects in its place (prisma 6.19.0, packages/client/src/runtime/core/extensions/resultUtils.ts, computeEngineSideSelection). What a literal does, read in prisma-engines 6.19.0: a relation filtered on null is a one-relation-is-null filter (query-engine/core/src/query_graph_builder/extractors/filters/relation.rs), which tests the link's own columns when they are in the filtered model's table (query-builders/sql-query-builder/src/filter/visitor.rs); among the nested writes (query-engine/core/src/query_graph_builder/write/nested/), connect with no finder returns before building a query, create, connectOrCreate, update, updateMany, upsert and deleteMany loop over the list they are handed, disconnect false returns on a one-to-one (on a one-to-many's to-one side the engine disconnects whatever the boolean), delete false deletes nothing, delete with an empty list, and disconnect with one on a one-to-many, still look the related rows up (their filter is an empty OR, so they find none) and change nothing, disconnect with an empty list on a many-to-many returns before building a query, createMany writes the rows its data lists, and set disconnects every linked row, then connects the rows it lists. Measured on Prisma 6.19.0 over SQLite: delete [] and a one-to-many disconnect [] send SELECT Post.id, Post.authorId ... WHERE (1=0 AND ...) and nothing else on Post; deleteMany [], create [] and createMany with data [] send nothing on Post. A result extension's needs read where a spread may add or replace its fields are not known.

examples.args: { where: { email: e }, select: { id: true, name: false } }
examples.why: a field selected false is not returned

examples.args: { where: { OR: [{ email: e }, { name: n }] } }
examples.why: no select: every scalar field is returned

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { name: n, posts: { create: [{ title: t }] } } }
examples.why: a nested write reaches another table, and says so

examples.args: { where: { accountId_date: { accountId, date } }, create: { accountId, date, value }, update: { value } }
examples.why: a compound unique key reads through the model's own compounds, not by splitting the key on _

examples.args: { where: { id_email: { a: 1, b: 2 } }, select: { id: true } }
examples.why: a named compound (@@unique([a, b], name: "id_email")) means a and b, never the id and email a split on _ would guess

examples.args: { where, select: { id: true } }
examples.why: a filter held in a variable has fields only the running program knows

examples.args: { by: ['date'], _count: true, _min: { value: true } }
{ ...query }
examples.why: a spread argument: which fields, and whether all of them are returned, is not known

examples.args: { [key]: { id: true } }
examples.why: a computed top-level key: which argument this call sends is not known, so it is not read as a select and the whole row is not claimed either

examples.args: { select: { id: true, email: flag } }
examples.why: a select value that is neither true nor false MAY be returned: the field is not dropped and not claimed EXACT, it goes to mayReads

examples.args: { include: { posts: true } }
examples.why: include returns every column of the related model, and the relation is followed into it

examples.args: { where: { id }, select: { email: true, posts: { where: { published: true }, select: { title: true } } } }
examples.why: a relation in a select is a find of its own on the related model: its where and its select are read there

examples.args: { select: { id: true, _count: { select: { posts: { where: { published: true } } } } } }
examples.why: _count counts the related rows a relation reaches, filtered by its own where

examples.args: { where: { posts: { some: { title: t } } } }
examples.why: a relation filter reads the related model's fields it filters on

examples.args: { where: { author: { email: e } } }
examples.why: a to-one relation filter may be written straight, with no is

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { posts: { create: [{ title: t }], deleteMany: { published: false } } } }
examples.why: each nested write is followed: a create writes the related row and sets the link, a deleteMany deletes the rows its filter reads

examples.args: { data: { title: t, author: { connect: { id: userId } } } }
examples.why: connect finds the related row by a unique field and sets the link: the related row is read, not written

examples.args: { include: { posts: withPosts } }
examples.why: an include value only the running program knows MAY read the relation: followed, and marked may, never claimed for certain

examples.args: { where: { author: null, reviewer: { isNot: null } }, select: { id: true } }
examples.why: a relation filtered on null only checks the link: which table that reads, the relation's own side or the other, is the schema's to say

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { posts: { create: [], connect: [], deleteMany: [] }, profile: { disconnect: false } } }
examples.why: an empty list creates, connects and deletes nothing; disconnect false does nothing on a one-to-one, which the schema says this relation is or is not

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { posts: { delete: [], disconnect: [], createMany: { data: [] } } } }
examples.why: measured on Prisma 6.19.0: delete [] and a one-to-many disconnect [] still select the children (Post.id, Post.authorId) and write nothing; a many-to-many disconnect [] and createMany with data [] send nothing

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { tags: { set: [] } } }
examples.why: set replaces the link; handed an empty list, it only clears it, which is still a write

examples.args: { select: { id: true, fullName: true } }
examples.why: a field the client's result extension computes reads what it needs, and is no column of its own
